questions.q:
The Samarkand City Library will survey its staff with a paper questionnaire and its readers with a Web questionnaire. You need at least 90 completed answers from each group.

  1. How many paper questionnaires must you hand out to staff? Give the best case and the worst case.
  2. How many readers must receive the Web questionnaire? Best case and worst case.
  3. A colleague sends the Web questionnaire to only 600 readers. How many answers can he expect? Is that enough?
questions.a:
Return rates: paper and e-mail 30–50%, Web often only 5–30%. People to send to = answers needed ÷ return rate.

  1. Paper: best case 90 ÷ 0.50 = 180; worst case 90 ÷ 0.30 = 300.
  2. Web: best case 90 ÷ 0.30 = 300; worst case 90 ÷ 0.05 = 1,800.
  3. 600 × 0.05 = 30 up to 600 × 0.30 = 180 answers. Only the best case gives enough. In the worst case he gets 30, far below 90. He should send it to more readers (up to 1,800) and raise the return rate: explain why the reader was chosen, give a return date, offer an inducement, offer a summary of the results.

questions.q:
A student drafted this questionnaire about the university canteen app. Find five problems, name the design guideline each one breaks, and fix it.

  • Name and student ID: ______
  • What is your family's monthly income?
  • Rate the UI of the CMS.
  • Wouldn't you agree that the old paper menu was terrible?
  • 40 more items on one page, jumping between prices, opening hours, app speed and prices again.
  • Last item: "Would you pay through the app if we built online payment?" (the question the project needs most)

None of the questions has a number.
questions.a:
ProblemGuideline brokenFix
Name and student ID requiredProvide anonymityRemove them; answers are anonymous.
Starts with family incomeBegin with nonthreatening and interesting questionsStart with "How often do you eat in the canteen?"; drop the income item.
"UI", "CMS"Avoid abbreviations"How easy is the app's menu screen to use?"
"Wouldn't you agree … terrible"Avoid biased or suggestive items"How satisfied were you with the paper menu? 1 = very unhappy … 5 = very happy."
Topics jump aroundGroup items into logically coherent sectionsSections: About you / Ordering / Payment.
40 items on one pageDo not crowd a pageSpread over several pages; cut repeated items.
Key question is lastDo not put important items at the very endMove it into the Payment section, early on.
No numbersNumber the questionsQ1, Q2, Q3 …

Any five of these are enough. Before sending: pretest it on a few students, and decide how the answers will be analyzed.

questions.q:
Classify each questionnaire item as a factual question or an opinion question. Then rewrite item (f) as a factual question.

  1. How many times did you order from the café app last week: 0, 1–2, 3–5, more than 5?
  2. Is the app easy to use?
  3. How long did your last order take to arrive: under 5 minutes, 5–10 minutes, more than 10 minutes?
  4. Do you agree that the delivery fee is too high?
  5. Which payment method did you use last time: cash, card, mobile wallet?
  6. Are app crashes common?
questions.a:
Factual (asks for a precise value): a, c, e.
Opinion (agree or disagree): b, d, f.

(f) rewritten: "How often does the app crash for you: once a day, once a week, once a month, never?"

All six are closed-ended. Questionnaires use closed-ended questions most, because nobody is there to help a confused respondent.

questions.q:
Which of these is NOT a ground rule of a JAD session?

A) Follow the schedule
B) Respect others' opinions
C) The facilitator casts the deciding vote when the group disagrees
D) Only one person talks at a time
questions.a: C, because the facilitator does not take part in the discussion and gives no ideas or opinions, so he stays neutral. The fourth real ground rule is "accept disagreement".

questions.q: Depict graphically the five steps of a JAD session. Add one key fact to each step and show who takes part.
questions.a:
Key labels to include:

  1. Select participants: by the information they can contribute; mix of organizational levels and political support; everyone must be away from the office at the same time.
  2. Design the session: half a day to several weeks, usually 5–10 days over 3 weeks; can build models or the requirements definition in the session.
  3. Prepare: often off-site; bring procedure manuals and documents, or think about improvements.
  4. Conduct: formal agenda and ground rules.
  5. Post-JAD follow-up: post-session report a week or two later (interview report: within 48 hours).

People: 10–20 users plus management and the project team, one neutral facilitator, 1–2 scribes (notes, often with CASE tools).
questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
  S1["1. Select participants: info they can give, mix of levels, political support"]
  S2["2. Design session: usually 5-10 days over 3 weeks"]
  S3["3. Prepare: often off-site, bring manuals and documents"]
  S4["4. Conduct: formal agenda and ground rules"]
  S5["5. Post-JAD follow-up: report in 1-2 weeks"]
  S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4 --> S5
  F(["Facilitator: neutral, guides"]) -.-> S4
  W(["1-2 scribes: notes, CASE tools"]) -.-> S4
  U(["10-20 users, management, project team"]) -.-> S4

questions.q:
A Tashkent bank wants a new loan-approval system. 15 loan officers, 3 branch managers and the IT team must agree on the new features. In a trial meeting, the junior officers stayed silent whenever the regional director spoke. A normal JAD would take 8 days over 3 weeks, and the branches cannot run without their staff that long.

  1. Which technique do you recommend, and why?
  2. If it saves 50–80% of the time, how many days would it take?
  3. Why not simply send a questionnaire?
questions.a:
1. e-JAD. Groupware lets every participant send ideas anonymously and at the same time, so junior officers have no fear of reprisal from the director. It keeps JAD's strengths: to-be information, High integration and High user involvement.
  2. 8 × 0.5 = 4 days; 8 × 0.2 = 1.6 days. So about 2–4 days, in line with the typical 1–4 days in one week. Staff are away from the branches for a shorter time.
  3. A questionnaire gives only as-is and improvements, with Medium depth and Low integration and user involvement. It cannot make the group agree on to-be features. It is meant for a large number of people or outside users, not about 20 insiders.

questions.q:
A city polyclinic is replacing phone appointments with an online booking system. Choose the best requirements-gathering technique for each situation, and give the reason from the techniques table.

  1. You want the opinions of 20,000 patients about phoning for appointments, and their ideas for improvements, at low cost.
  2. The head doctor, nurses, receptionists and IT must agree on the new system's features and draft the requirements together.
  3. The receptionists' paper appointment books and three years of referral forms are kept in a cupboard.
  4. The head receptionist says no patient waits more than 10 minutes at the desk, but patients complain.
  5. Only one IT engineer knows the rules linking the old system to the national insurance database.
questions.a:
1. Questionnaire: large number of people (patients are outside users); breadth High, cost Low; gives as-is and improvements. Use a sample and expect low returns.
  2. JAD: to-be information; the only technique with High integration and High user involvement; cost Low–Medium; requirements can be built in the session.
  3. Document analysis: as-is, breadth High, cost Low. Look for information staff added by hand.
  4. Observation: shows what really happens and checks the validity of what people said.
  5. Interview: depth High, can give to-be information; only one person, so breadth (Low) does not matter and the Medium cost is acceptable.

questions.q:
An analyst needs information from many people at low cost, and also wants their ideas for improvements, but does not need ideas for the to-be system. According to the techniques table, which technique fits best?

A) Observation
B) Document analysis
C) Questionnaires
D) JAD
questions.a: C, because questionnaires have High breadth, Low cost and give as-is and improvements. Document analysis gives as-is only, observation has Low breadth, and JAD has only Medium breadth.

questions.q:
An analyst at a pharmacy chain reviews 200 completed customer intake forms and the reports staff use. She notices:

  1. Pharmacists write the customer's allergies in the margin.
  2. The "Date" field is filled in three different formats.
  3. Cashiers keep their own notebook of customers waiting for out-of-stock medicines.
  4. Every Monday the manager opens three different reports to see stock of popular medicines.

What does each finding tell her? Which findings are the strongest sign that the system must change? Why should she look at blank forms as well as completed ones?
questions.a:
1. A field is missing: add an "Allergies" field.
  2. The field is unclear: show the format (DD.MM.YYYY) or use a date picker.
  3. Users made their own form: the system needs a waiting-list (back-order) function.
  4. One need takes several reports: new information or a new format is needed, e.g. one stock report.

Strongest sign: 1 and 3. When users create their own forms or add extra information to existing ones, that is the most powerful indication the system needs to change.

The blank form shows how the form was designed; the completed forms show how people really use it. The changes show up in the gap between the two.

questions.q:
(a) Using the techniques table, compare interviews and observation on type of information, depth and cost.
(b) Give two reasons an analyst still observes after interviewing.
(c) Ethnography: what does it reveal, what is one weakness, and what is focused ethnography?
questions.a:
(a)

InterviewsObservation
Type of informationAs-is, improvements, to-beAs-is only
DepthHighLow
CostMediumLow to Medium

(b) In interviews people describe their work, and many managers do not remember how they really work or spend their time. Observation shows the reality and checks the validity of information from indirect sources (interviews, questionnaires).

(c) Ethnography reveals how people actually work (not how they ought to), and how cooperation and awareness of others' work shape it. Weakness: it cannot identify new features, and it may study practices that are no longer relevant. Focused ethnography = ethnography + prototyping (from an air traffic control project): questions raised by the prototype focus what you observe.

questions.q: Depict graphically a decision path an analyst can follow to choose among the five requirements-gathering techniques.
questions.a: Key points: to-be information comes only from interviews or JAD; choose JAD when many people must agree (High integration and user involvement) and interviews for depth from a few key people; questionnaires for breadth at low cost; document analysis when forms, manuals and reports exist (as-is); observation to see reality and check what people said. In real projects analysts combine several techniques.

  F["Questionnaire: breadth High, cost Low"]

questions.q:
A reviewer reads the requirements for a new university library system. For each finding, name the check that fails (Validity, Consistency, Completeness, Realism, Verifiability). Finding (f) fails a review check instead: which one?

  1. "The search must respond quickly."
  2. R3: "Fines are charged in UZS." R11: "Fines are charged in USD."
  3. The library asked for e-book lending, but no requirement mentions it.
  4. "Face recognition at every shelf, built in 2 weeks for $1,000."
  5. The library's main problem is lost books, but the requirements describe a social network for readers.
  6. Nobody knows who asked for the "dark mode" requirement, or why.
questions.a:
1. Verifiability: "quickly" cannot be checked. Better: "search results appear within 2 seconds".
  2. Consistency: two requirements conflict.
  3. Completeness: a function the customer needs is missing.
  4. Realism: cannot be built with this budget and technology.
  5. Validity: the functions do not support the customer's real need.
  6. Traceability (review check): the origin of the requirement is not stated.

questions.q:
The team ran a questionnaire with 400 students. In which section of the system proposal should the full questionnaire results go?

A) Requirements Definition
B) Appendices
C) Executive Summary
D) Feasibility Analysis
questions.a: B, because Appendices hold supporting material such as questionnaire or interview results. The Requirements Definition lists the functional and nonfunctional requirements drawn from them, not the raw results.

questions.q:
System proposal: give the section (number and name) where each item belongs.

  1. The revised cost–benefit analysis with NPV
  2. A one-page overview so the busy rector can decide what to read in depth
  3. The revised Gantt chart
  4. "The system must be available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week."
  5. The use-case diagram and use case descriptions
  6. CRC cards and the class diagram
  7. The CRUDE matrix and sequence diagrams
  8. The updated business need and sponsor
  9. Notes from 12 interviews
questions.a:
1. 5 Feasibility Analysis (revised)
  2. 2 Executive Summary
  3. 4 Workplan (revised)
  4. 6 Requirements Definition (a nonfunctional requirement)
  5. 7 Functional Model
  6. 8 Structural Models
  7. 9 Behavioral Models
  8. 3 System Request (revised)
  9. 10 Appendices

Section 1 is the Table of Contents.

questions.q: Depict graphically the structure of the system proposal: all ten sections in order, grouped in a sensible way, and who receives the document.
questions.a: Key labels: Openers: 1 Table of Contents, 2 Executive Summary. Revised planning documents: 3 System Request, 4 Workplan, 5 Feasibility Analysis. New analysis results: 6 Requirements Definition, 7 Functional Model (activity diagram, use cases), 8 Structural Models (CRC cards, class and object diagrams), 9 Behavioral Models (sequence and communication diagrams, state machines, CRUDE matrix). Then 10 Appendices. The proposal goes to the approval committee.

Sort these terms into the three lists: requirements checks, validation techniques and review checks. One term belongs in two lists.

Traceability · Prototyping · Realism · Adaptability · Test-case generation · Consistency · Comprehensibility · Requirements reviews · Completeness · Validity · Verifiability

Verifiability is in both check lists: "can the requirements be checked?" and "is it realistically testable?"

questions.q:
The canteen app went live in September. Since then:

  1. A new law requires an electronic fiscal receipt for every sale.
  2. The university administration, which paid for the app, refused online payment to save money, but students keep asking for it.
  3. Students want a vegetarian filter and many menu options; kitchen staff want a short, simple menu. The old compromise no longer works.

(1) Name the reason for the requirements change in each case. (2) What does requirements management do about such changes? (3) Fixing an implementation error costs $150. Up to how much could a requirements error found after delivery cost?
questions.a:
(1)

  1. The business and technical environment changes after installation (here, new laws and regulations).
  2. The people who pay are rarely the people who use the system; the payer's budget limits conflict with users' needs, so features get added after delivery.
  3. Large systems have diverse users with conflicting priorities; the requirements are a compromise, and the balance has to change.

(2) It keeps track of each requirement, keeps links between dependent requirements so the impact of a change can be seen, and uses a formal process for change proposals.

(3) Up to 100 × $150 = $15,000. That is why requirements are validated early.
